name: Tonka bean

card.summary: The coumarin-rich seed of Dipteryx odorata, used as a sweet, vanilla-almond note in perfumes and colognes to give a pleasant personal scent.
card.note: Ingesting the bean is restricted in some countries because of coumarin; fragrance use is the grooming context.

quick.overview:
Tonka bean is the seed of a South American tree whose scent comes from coumarin. In grooming it appears as a warm, sweet, vanilla-like base note in many colognes and men's fragrances, adding to how a person smells and is perceived.

It matters to looks mainly as part of fragrance and grooming rather than as a treatment: it is an ingredient in scents, and research on it concerns the chemistry of coumarins rather than any effect on appearance.
quick.how: People encounter it as a listed note (often "tonka") in perfumes, aftershaves and body sprays, worn on the skin after showering as part of a grooming routine. It is used as a fragrance ingredient, not applied or eaten as a looks product.
quick.risks: Coumarin can irritate or sensitise some skin types; large oral doses are linked to liver toxicity, and since 1954 the US FDA has treated foods containing tonka beans as adulterated.[1]

lead: Tonka bean is the seed of Dipteryx odorata, a tree native to northern South America. Its seeds typically contain about 1 to 3 percent coumarin, which gives the bean a sweet, hay-and-vanilla scent.[1][2]

Perfumers use tonka or synthetic coumarin as a base note in fragrances, including men's scents; one cited example is Yves Rocher's Hoggar.[1] For someone working on grooming, scent is one more part of presentation alongside hair, skin and clothing.

Coumarin was first isolated from the bean in 1820, and the name derives from the French term for it, coumarou.[2][3] Published research concerns coumarin chemistry and analysis rather than cosmetic outcomes.[6]

paras: The tree is in the pea family, and its seeds smell like sweet woodruff.[1] The name tonka comes from the Galibi (Carib) language of French Guiana.[1]

Coumarin gives a sweet, almond-vanilla warmth that perfumers use for depth, and tonka features as a note in men's colognes.[1] Artificial coumarin was synthesised in the 1940s and became an early artificial flavouring and vanilla substitute.[1]

Tonka extracts contain coumarin, dihydrocoumarin and melilotic-acid compounds, and the solvent used to extract them changes the mix found.[6] Reviews of natural coumarins trace the family back to this seed.[2][3]

Large doses of coumarin may cause liver damage, and many governments regulate it as a food additive. Coumarin itself is not an anticoagulant; warfarin derives from a related compound.[1][7] The FDA has treated foods containing tonka beans as adulterated since 1954; enthusiasts import the beans anyway.[1]

No studies found on tonka bean as a cosmetic or grooming product. Related laboratory work covers coumarin derivatives in cancer-chemoprevention and platelet research, and a food-science study examined roasted tonka beans nutritionally.[4][7][5]
